w: This is where the King does business, not where he lives - the royal family actually resides at Laeken, up the road. The grand facade only rose after 1900 under Leopold II, on ground that was once part of the medieval Coudenberg Palace. Inside: state rooms for receptions, offices for the actual work of monarchy.
s: The king's palace - but he doesn't sleep here
_facts: Official palace of the King and Queen but not their residence (they live at the Royal Palace of Laeken)
Present facade built after 1900 on the initiative of King Leopold II
Grounds were once part of the medieval Palace of Coudenberg

w: Josef Hoffmann's 1911 masterpiece for financier Adolphe Stoclet, built as a Vienna Secession 'total work of art' down to a dress designed so Madame Stoclet wouldn't clash with the decor. The family still owns it and still won't let anyone inside, not even restorers. UNESCO-listed since 2009 - admire it from the street.
s: Vienna Secession jewel you can only see from the street
_facts: Designed by Josef Hoffmann for financier Adolphe Stoclet, built 1905-1911 in Vienna Secession style
Not open to visitors; historically not even restoration experts were admitted
UNESCO World Heritage Site since June 2009

w: An hour before the 1985 European Cup final, Juventus fans were crushed against a wall here fleeing charging Liverpool supporters - it gave way, and 39 died, most of them Italian. Inspectors had already flagged the stadium as unsafe. Demolished, rebuilt as King Baudouin Stadium; the disaster still shapes crowd policing.
s: The wall that collapsed before the 1985 European Cup final
_facts: 29 May 1985, before the Juventus-Liverpool European Cup final
39 spectators killed, mostly Italian Juventus fans, when a wall collapsed under crowd pressure as they fled an attack by Liverpool fans
Stadium had failed safety inspections beforehand; later rebuilt as King Baudouin Stadium

n: Cathedral of St. Michael and St. Gudula
w: Started as a Romanesque chapel in the 11th century, rebuilt in stages until the 16th, this is Brabantine Gothic at its grandest - twin pipe organs, immense bells, chapels stacked up over centuries. Cathedral since 1962, it's where Belgium holds royal weddings, state funerals and the National Day Te Deum.
s: Brussels' Gothic showpiece, five centuries in the making
_facts: Construction began 11th century, largely complete in Gothic form by the 16th century
Major example of Brabantine Gothic architecture; two pipe organs and historic bells
Became a cathedral in 1962; hosts royal weddings, state funerals, and the National Day Te Deum

n: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium
w: Six museums under one roof - Old Masters, Magritte, Fin-de-Siecle, Modern, Wiertz, Meunier - hold more than 20,000 works from the 15th century to now, including Bruegel, Van Dyck and Rubens. The Magritte Museum alone claims the world's largest Rene Magritte collection, making this Belgium's most-visited art complex.
s: Six museums, one address, Bruegel to Magritte
_facts: Group of six museums: Oldmasters, Magritte, Fin-de-Siecle, Modern, Wiertz, Meunier museums
Over 20,000 works spanning 15th century to present, including Bruegel, van der Weyden, van Dyck, Jordaens, Rubens
Magritte Museum houses the world's largest collection of Rene Magritte's work; most-visited art institution in Belgium

n: National Basilica of the Sacred Heart
w: Leopold II laid the first stone in 1905; two world wars later, this Art Deco mountain finally opened in 1970 as the 17th-largest church on Earth and the biggest in Belgium. Modeled on Paris's Sacre-Coeur, its green copper dome climbs 89 metres above the Koekelberg plateau - everyone just calls it 'the Koekelberg.'
_facts: First stone laid by Leopold II in 1905; construction halted by both World Wars, finished 1970
17th largest church by area in the world, largest in Belgium
Art Deco style with neo-Byzantine inspiration; copper dome rises 89 metres; popularly known as Koekelberg Basilica

w: Raised between 1401 and 1455, this is the sole medieval survivor on the Grand-Place, a masterpiece of Brabantine Gothic facing down the neo-Gothic King's House across the square. Its three classicist rear wings were tacked on centuries later. Still the working seat of city government, and UNESCO-listed since 1998.
s: The only medieval building left on the Grand-Place
_facts: Built 1401-1455; only remaining medieval building on the Grand-Place
Considered a masterpiece of civil Gothic / Brabantine Gothic architecture
UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998, as part of the Grand-Place
